name: Roberts Solution and Critical Collapse
description: A massless scalar field falling in from infinity onto empty space, an exact solution of Einstein's equations that Mark Roberts found as a counterexample to cosmic censorship. It looks the same at every scale, and one number $p$ decides how it ends: for $p < 1$ the field passes through the centre and leaves flat space behind, for $p > 1$ it makes a black hole, and at $p = 1$ it leaves a null singularity.
convention:
The parameter $p$ is a pure number, and the scalar field $\varphi$ is scaled so that Einstein's equations read $R_{\mu
u} = 2\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_
u\varphi$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu
u} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha
u}$.
history: Can a singularity form in plain sight, with no horizon to hide it? Roger Penrose's cosmic censorship hypothesis says no, and Mark Roberts went looking for a yes [penrose1969, roberts1989]. The static solutions with a massless scalar field already have a singularity and no horizon, but it is there from the start, so he wanted one that develops [roberts1996]. In flat spacetime the field has the spherical solution $\varphi = \sigma(v)/r$, a wave whose strength $\sigma(v)$ can start at zero and then grow [roberts1996]. Roberts found the solution of Einstein's equations that does the same with gravity switched on, in his thesis of 1986 and in print in 1989, under the title "Scalar field counterexamples to the cosmic censorship hypothesis" [roberts1996, roberts1989]. Its energy adds up to nothing: "the positive energy of the scalar field and the negative energy of the gravitational field cancel out" [roberts1996].¶Four years later Matthew Choptuik sent pulses of the same massless field inward on a computer and turned one knob, call it $p$, that set how strong the pulse was [choptuik1993, gundlach2007]. A weak pulse passes through the centre and disperses, and a strong one makes a black hole [gundlach2007]. Tuning $p$ toward the threshold $p_*$, he could make black holes as small as he liked, with a mass proportional to $(p - p_*)^{\gamma}$ and $\gamma \simeq 0.37$ for every family of pulses he tried [choptuik1993, gundlach2007]. On the threshold itself the solution repeats its own shape on ever smaller scales, once for every $\Delta \simeq 3.44$ in the logarithm of the scale [gundlach2007].¶Could any of that be done with pencil and paper? Patrick Brady, in December 1993, and Yoshimi Oshiro, Kouji Nakamura, and Akira Tomimatsu, a month later, assumed that the collapse looks the same at every scale and solved the equations exactly [brady1994, oshiro1994]. Their solution has one number $p$: below $p = 1$ the field falls in, passes through the centre, and leaves flat space behind, and above it an apparent horizon forms around a spacelike singularity [oshiro1994, brady1994]. At $p = 1$ the singularity lies along a light ray and no horizon forms [brady1994]. Just above the threshold the mass inside the apparent horizon grows as $(p - 1)^{1/2}$, a power law as Choptuik's was, though his exponent was $0.37$ [oshiro1994, brady1994]. Brady had finished when Werner Israel told him the solution was Roberts's [brady1994].¶A black hole made this way never stops growing, since the field keeps arriving forever [brady1994]. Anzhong Wang and Henrique de Oliveira mended that in 1997: they cut the spacetime along a light ray and joined it to Vaidya's radiating solution, which leaves a hole of finite mass and the same exponent $1/2$ [wang1997collapse]. That year Lior Burko put the double null form in Roberts's paper back into the field equations and found that it solves them only for $\sigma = 0$ and $\sigma = -1$ [burko1997]. The slip was in the change of coordinates, and the correct double null form is Oshiro, Nakamura, and Tomimatsu's, with $p = 2\sigma$ [burko1997].¶Is $p = 1$ the solution on Choptuik's threshold, then? Roberts's solution looks the same at every scale, and Choptuik's only at scales a factor $e^{\Delta}$ apart [gundlach2007]. A solution on the threshold has one growing perturbation and no more, the one that tips it toward a black hole or toward dispersal [gundlach2007]. The perturbation equations of the $p = 1$ solution can be solved exactly, and when Andrei Frolov did so in 1997 he found growing modes filling a whole region of the complex plane, so it cannot be the critical solution [frolov1997, gundlach2007]. Perturbations that break the spherical symmetry all decay [frolov1999]. Frolov then proposed that the fastest growing mode carries Roberts's solution over into Choptuik's, with the mode's oscillation becoming the echo [frolov2000, gundlach2007].¶As for cosmic censorship, the answer for this field is Demetrios Christodoulou's: a collapsing massless scalar field can make a naked singularity, his theorem of 1994, but the initial data that do so are not generic, his theorem of 1999 [christodoulou1994, christodoulou1999, gundlach2007]. Data tuned to the threshold are special in just that way, with one number set exactly, and Choptuik's critical solution has a naked singularity at its centre [gundlach2007]. Roberts's singularity at $p = 1$ sits on the light ray $u = 0$, where the mass goes to zero and the curvature diverges [brady1994]. Brady wrote that "no observer can see the singularity without actually reaching it" [brady1994].

related.text: Roberts's solution with the field switched off, $p = 0$. Flat space is also what the field falls onto, before its first ray $v = 0$, and for $p < 1$ what it leaves behind, after $u = 0$ [oshiro1994, brady1994].
The same massless scalar field standing still. Its singularity is there from the start, which is why Roberts went looking for a solution that moves [roberts1996].

Anzhong Wang and Henrique de Oliveira cut Roberts's collapse along a light ray and joined it to Vaidya's outgoing radiation, which gives the black hole a finite mass [wang1997collapse]. Let the field's strength $pv/2$ be any function $\alpha(v)$ and Roberts's metric still solves Einstein's equations, with null dust like Vaidya's flowing in beside the scalar field [roberts1996].

A static soliton on a threshold of collapse. For a Yang-Mills field Choptuik, Chmaj, and Bizoń found black holes that begin at a finite mass, with the first Bartnik-McKinnon soliton as the critical solution [choptuik1996].

coordinates.name: Double Null
domains: v = 0 \;\text{(the field's first ray, flat space before it)}

parameters.description: Strength of the incoming field, a pure number with $p \ge 0$: the field disperses for $p < 1$ and makes a black hole for $p > 1$; Roberts's $\sigma$ is $p/2$

coordinates.convention: We use the retarded and advanced null coordinates $(u, v)$, both lengths, with $R$ the areal radius, $R^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}\left((1-p^2)v^2 - 2uv + u^2\right)$. The field is $\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(((1-p)v - u)/((1+p)v - u)\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

nonzero.value: \dfrac{\left(1 - p^2\right)v - u}{\left(\left(1 - p\right)v - u\right)\left(\left(1 + p\right)v - u\right)}

geodesics: \ddot{\theta} - \dfrac{2v - 2u}{\left(\left(1 - p\right)v - u\right)\left(\left(1 + p\right)v - u\right)}\dot{u}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2\left(\left(1 - p^2\right)v - u\right)}{\left(\left(1 - p\right)v - u\right)\left(\left(1 + p\right)v - u\right)}\dot{v}\dot{\theta} - \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{\phi} - \dfrac{2v - 2u}{\left(\left(1 - p\right)v - u\right)\left(\left(1 + p\right)v - u\right)}\dot{u}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{2\left(\left(1 - p^2\right)v - u\right)}{\left(\left(1 - p\right)v - u\right)\left(\left(1 + p\right)v - u\right)}\dot{v}\dot{\phi} + 2\cot\theta\,\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} = 0

coordinates.name: Roberts
domains: v = 0 \;\text{(the field's first ray, flat space before it)}
r = p(1+p)v/2 \;\text{(the apparent horizon, for } p > 1\text{)}

parameters.description: Strength of the incoming field, a pure number with $p \ge 0$: the field disperses for $p < 1$ and makes a black hole for $p > 1$; Roberts's $\sigma$ is $p/2$

coordinates.convention: We use Roberts's coordinates $(v, r)$, both lengths, with $v$ the advanced null coordinate and $r = ((1+p)v - u)/2$ for the retarded null coordinate $u$. The areal radius is $R = \sqrt{r(r - pv)}$ and the field is $\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1 - pv/r)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Areal Radius
domains: v = 0 \;\text{(the field's first ray, flat space before it)}
R = p\sqrt{p^2-1}\,v/2 \;\text{(the apparent horizon, for } p > 1\text{)}

parameters.description: Strength of the incoming field, a pure number with $p \ge 0$: the field disperses for $p < 1$ and makes a black hole for $p > 1$; Roberts's $\sigma$ is $p/2$
Roberts's $\lambda$, a length: his coordinate $r$ is $\lambda + pv/2$

coordinates.convention: We use the advanced null coordinate $v$ and the areal radius $R$, both lengths, and write $\lambda = \sqrt{R^2 + p^2v^2/4}$. The field is $\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left((2\lambda - pv)/(2\lambda + pv)\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Time and Radius
domains: ct = -\rho \;\text{(the field's first ray, flat space before it)}

parameters.description: Strength of the incoming field, a pure number with $p \ge 0$: the field disperses for $p < 1$ and makes a black hole for $p > 1$; Roberts's $\sigma$ is $p/2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ a length. The areal radius is $R = \sqrt{\rho(\rho - pct)}$ and the field is $\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1 - pct/\rho)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Scaling
domains: x = 0 \;\text{(the field's first ray, flat space before it)}

parameters.description: Strength of the incoming field, a pure number with $p \ge 0$: the field disperses for $p < 1$ and makes a black hole for $p > 1$; Roberts's $\sigma$ is $p/2$
Any length, the unit $u$ and $v$ are counted in

coordinates.convention: We use the scaling coordinates $(\tau, x)$, both pure numbers, with $u = -2\ell e^{-\tau}$ and $v = \ell e^{-\tau}(e^{2x} - 1)$ for the null coordinates $u$ and $v$. The areal radius is $R = \ell e^{x-\tau}\sqrt{\cosh^2x - p^2\sinh^2x}$ and the field is $\varphi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left((1 - p\tanh x)/(1 + p\tanh x)\right)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
